title: Why workflow?
text:
Conditions for Reproducibility
To achieve reproducibility, we need to control several factors:

title: Why workflow?
text:
Data: Use the exact same data. This often means versioning your data or ensuring it’s immutable.
Code: Every data wrangling step and output (summaries, plots, analyses) must be generated via code, executed in the same sequence. No manual tweaks!
Environment: This is crucial. You need the same version of R, and critically, the same versions of all the R packages you used. Different package versions can behave differently, leading to different results.

Technical methods to keep the environment the same (as much as possible): dependencies lockfiles, Docker containers, fixed random seeds.

Version Control: Keeping track of changes to your data, code, and environment configurations. (We’ll dive deeper into this next week with Git!)

title: Why workflow?
text:
Conditions for Reusability (Brief Introduction)
For reusability, we focus on flexibility and adaptability:

Understandable Code: Well-documented, commented, and clearly structured so you know where to tweak it for different inputs.
Handles Altered Inputs: Your code should reliably process new data, ideally with checks and conditions to flag unexpected inputs.
Environment: Able to behave as intended across a broad range of environments (e.g., minimal package requirements, compatible with many package versions).

Quick comparison of these two concepts:








Feature
Reproducible Workflow
Reusable Workflow




Data
Identical data (versioned, locked, immutable).
New/altered data (validated upon entry).


Code
Strict execution order, hardcoded random seeds.
Modular, heavily parameterized, well-documented.


Environment
Strictly locked down to the exact patch version.
Broadly compatible across a wide range of versions.



We’ll focus on reproducibility today, and then next week we’ll really dig into the hands-on aspects of making things reusable.

title: Environment Management in R
text:
Step 0: Start a New RStudio Project
You learned about RStudio Projects (.Rproj) back in Week 1. As a quick recap:
Why do we always start with a Project? Because it fixes your working directory to this folder, keeping all your files, data, and scripts self-contained. This is the same reason renv works on a per-project basis. Each project gets its own isolated package library, so projects never interfere with each other.

title: Environment Management in R
text:
In RStudio, go to File → New Project → New Directory → New Project.
Name it something like week3-renv-practice, and choose a location on your computer.
Click Create Project. RStudio will reopen in this new project, and you’ll see a week3-renv-practice.Rproj file in your file pane.

title: Environment Management in R
text:
Step 1: Install and Initialize renv
If you don’t already have renv installed, install it once (this is the only package you install the “normal” way for this exercise):
install.packages("renv")
Now, inside your new project, initialize renv:
renv::init()
What just happened? Check your file pane. You should now see:

A new renv/ folder (this stores the project’s private package library).
A renv.lock file (currently a near-empty lockfile).
A .Rprofile file has been created or updated. This is what automatically activates renv every time you open this project. You may see a message asking renv to scan your project for package dependencies. Since your project is empty right now, it likely won’t find anything yet.

title: Environment Management in R
section: Step 2: Install Some Packages and Write Some Code
text:
Step 2: Install Some Packages and Write Some Code
Let’s simulate a real workflow. Install a couple of packages you’d normally use:
install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2"))
Create a new R script called analysis.R in your project, and add a few lines that use these packages:
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# A tiny example dataset
df <- data.frame(
  group = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  value = c(10, 15, 20, 25)
)

summary_df <- df %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(mean_value = mean(value))

print(summary_df)

ggplot(df, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot()
Run the script (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + S or source it line-by-line) to make sure it works.

title: Environment Management in R
text:
Step 3: Take Your First Snapshot
Now that you’ve installed packages and written code that uses them, “snapshot” your environment. This tells renv to record the exact versions of dplyr, ggplot2, and their dependencies into renv.lock:
renv::snapshot()
renv will scan your project files, detect which packages are actually used in your code, and ask you to confirm before writing to the lockfile. Type y and press Enter.
Open renv.lock (it’s a plain text/JSON file) and take a look. You’ll see entries like this for each package:
"dplyr": {
  "Package": "dplyr",
  "Version": "1.1.4",
  "Source": "Repository",
  "Repository": "CRAN"
}
This is your “receipt” of exactly which package versions your analysis depends on.

title: Environment Management in R
text:
Step 4: Update Your Snapshot
Workflows evolve. Let’s add one more package and update the lockfile accordingly.
install.packages("tidyr")
Add a line to analysis.R that uses it. (It doesn’t need to do anything meaningful. This is just practice):
library(tidyr)
Save the script, then snapshot again:
renv::snapshot()
Check renv.lock again. you should now see tidyr added to the file alongside dplyr and ggplot2.
Checkpoint: Every time you add, remove, or update a package your project depends on, you should re-run renv::snapshot() to keep the lockfile in sync with reality.

title: Environment Management in R
text:
Step 5: Close the Session
Now, fully close RStudio (not just the project). Quit the application entirely. This simulates what happens when you come back to a project days or weeks later, or hand it off to someone else.

title: Environment Management in R
text:
Step 6: Reopen and Restore
Reopen RStudio by double-clicking the .Rproj file. Because of the .Rprofile that renv::init() set up, renv will automatically activate for this project. You may see a message in the console about renv being active.
To restore the exact package versions recorded in renv.lock, run:
renv::restore()
renv will compare the lockfile against your project’s private library and install anything that’s missing or mismatched. Since nothing has changed, it will likely report that the library is already in sync.
Try this: To really see renv::restore() in action, manually delete the renv/library folder inside your project folder (not the whole renv/ folder, just library), then run renv::restore() again. Watch as it reinstalls the exact versions listed in renv.lock from scratch.

You now have a project where:
renv.lock is a precise, shareable record of every package version your analysis depends on. Anyone who receives your project folder (including the renv.lock file) can run renv::restore() and get the exact same package environment.

text:
Now it’s your turn!

Exercise 3.1:
Revise the R script you wrote in week 2 such that it becomes a reproducible workflow. This means:

Start a new RStudio Project for this week’s work.
Initialize renv in your new project using renv::init().
Copy your Week 2 R script (Exercise 2.2) into this new project.
Ensure your script runs from start to finish without errors, covering data import, wrangling, summary, analysis, and visualization.
Snapshot your renv environment using renv::snapshot() once your script is finalized and all necessary packages are installed.

title: Version Control via Git
text:
Sharing Code: The Wrong Way(s) and the Right Way
Think about how you might share an R script with a classmate or colleague. Chances are it looks something like one of these:

title: Version Control via Git
text:
Emailing scripts back and forth. It’s hard to track which version of code was used to generate what results, and nobody can say for certain which copy is the current one. Email attachments also strip away your folder structure, which you now know is essential for reproducibility.
Putting files in a synced drive (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, etc.). It’s hard to track when things get changed, by whom, and for what reason. There’s no clear trace of changes, which makes it challenging to revert cleanly when something breaks.


Advantages of Version Control

Complete history: Every change is recorded, along with who made it, when, and (ideally) why.
Safe experimentation: You can try out new approaches on “branches” without risking your working code.
Collaboration: Multiple people can work on the same project simultaneously, and Git provides tools to merge everyone’s changes together sensibly.
Accountability and reproducibility: Combined with what you learned about renv last section, Git lets you say precisely “this exact version of the code, with this exact environment, produced this exact result.”

title: Version Control via Git
text:
What is Git?
Git is a distributed version control system (DVCS). In plain terms: it’s a tool that takes periodic “snapshots” of your project folder (called commits), and keeps a complete history of those snapshots so you can inspect, compare, or revert to any of them at any time.
The word distributed matters. In older, centralized version control systems, there was one central server holding the “real” history, and everyone’s computer held just the files they were currently working on. If the central server went down, nobody could see the project history. With Git, every single person who clones a project gets the entire history, on their own machine. There is no single point of failure, and you can commit, branch, and review history even while offline. (see Conceptual diagram.)
In everyday use, Git tracks your files through a simple pipeline: changes you make live in your working directory, you selectively mark the changes you want to record using git add (moving them to the staging area), and then git commit permanently saves that snapshot into your local repository. Whenever you’re ready to share your work, git push sends your commits to a remote repository that others can access, and git pull (or git fetch) brings down commits that others have made.





flowchart LR
    A[Working Directory] -->|git add| B[Staging Area]
    B -->|git commit| C[Local Repository]
    C -->|git push| D[Remote Repository\ne.g. GitHub]
    D -->|git pull| C


 Git’s basic workflow: staging, committing, and syncing with a remote (adapted from the Pro Git book, git-scm.com).

title: Version Control via Git
section: What is GitHub? Is It the Only Option?
text:
What is GitHub? Is It the Only Option?
Git itself is just a program that runs on your computer. It does not require the Internet, and it does not require GitHub. GitHub is a separate, web-based hosting service for Git repositories. It stores a copy of your repository “in the cloud” so that you and your collaborators have a shared, always-available remote to push to and pull from, plus a web interface for browsing code, discussing changes, and managing projects.
GitHub is simply the most popular option, but it isn’t the only one. Alternatives you’ll encounter include GitLab and Bitbucket, which offer similar hosting with their own features, and many organizations (hospitals, universities, government agencies working with sensitive health data) run their own self-hosted Git servers. You can even push and pull between two personal computers directly, with no hosting service involved at all, since Git fundamentally only needs a reachable file location to treat as a “remote.” For this course, we’ll use GitHub because of its popularity, its free tier for public and private repositories, and its gentle integration with RStudio.

title: Version Control via Git
text:
Setting up GitHub

Step 1: Sign Up for a GitHub Account
If you don’t already have one, create a free account at github.com. Use an email address you’ll have long-term access to (not one tied to an employer or school you might leave), since this account will likely follow your work for years.


Step 2: Install Git and Connect It to RStudio

Install Git on your computer, if it isn’t already installed:

Windows: Download and install from git-scm.com.
Mac: Install via Xcode Command Line Tools (run xcode-select --install in Terminal) or download from git-scm.com.

Open RStudio and go to Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN. Confirm that RStudio has correctly detected the path to your Git executable.
Tell Git who you are (run once, in the RStudio Terminal tab, not the R console):
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your_email@example.com"
Use the same email address as your GitHub account so your commits are correctly linked to your profile.
Set up authentication between RStudio and GitHub. GitHub no longer accepts your account password for this; instead, you’ll generate a Personal Access Token (PAT). The usethis R package makes this painless:
install.packages("usethis")
usethis::create_github_token()   # opens GitHub in your browser to generate a token
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()         # paste the token here to store it securely

For a more detailed, well-regarded walkthrough of this entire setup process, Jenny Bryan’s online guide Happy Git and GitHub for the useR is an excellent free resource, and is used in many university-level R courses. The RStudio documentation on version control with Git is also a concise companion reference.


Step 3: Create Your First Repository

Open the RStudio Project you want to turn into a Git repository (for example, your week3-renv-practice project, or a fresh project with your analysis.R script from Exercise 3.1). In the R console, run:
usethis::use_git()
You’ll be asked whether to commit all existing files as a first commit, type 1 for Yes. RStudio will then restart the project. Once it reopens, you should see a new Git pane (top right, next to Environment/History), confirming your project is now a Git repository.
Push this repository to GitHub, creating the remote copy, directly from R:
usethis::use_github()
This creates a new repository under your GitHub account with the same name as your project, links it to your local repo, and pushes your commit(s) up in one step. When it finishes, your repository’s URL will print in the console; open it in your browser to confirm your files are there. By default this creates a public repository, which is what you want for this exercise so your friend can access it.
If use_github() doesn’t work for you (for example, if authentication isn’t configured correctly), you can instead create the repository manually: go to github.com, click the + icon (top right) → New repository, give it a name, keep it Public, and click Create repository (leave “Add a README” unticked, since your project already has files). GitHub will show you a page with commands under “…or push an existing repository from the command line”; copy the two git remote add origin ... and git push ... lines and run them in RStudio’s Terminal tab.
Add or edit a file (for example, edit the README.md, or confirm your analysis.R script is present). Then, in RStudio’s Git pane, tick the checkbox next to the changed file(s) to stage them, click Commit, write a short commit message describing what changed, and click Commit again.
Click Push (the green up-arrow icon) to send your commit up to GitHub.
Send the repository link to a friend. They can clone it themselves (File → New Project → Version Control → Git in their own RStudio, pasting in your repository’s URL from the green Code button on GitHub) or, if you add them as a collaborator (Settings → Collaborators on GitHub), they can push changes back too.
When your friend makes changes and pushes them, click Pull (the blue down-arrow icon) in your own RStudio Git pane to bring their changes down into your local copy.

A note on the commit hash: After committing, look at the History view in the Git pane (the clock icon). Each commit is labeled with a hash. You can always reference a specific commit by this hash, which is how you’d tell someone exactly which version of your project to check out or restore.

Every commit you make is given a unique identifier called a hash (something like a3f5c9e..., a long string of letters and numbers). This hash isn’t arbitrary. It’s generated from the content of the commit itself, so even the tiniest change to your code produces a completely different hash. This is actually a core part of what makes Git trustworthy for reproducibility: you can tell someone “run commit a3f5c9e” and know, with certainty, they are running the exact same code you ran, not some similar-looking copy.



Step 4: Comments and Issues on GitHub
GitHub isn’t just for code storage. It includes lightweight project management tools built around your repository:

Comments on commits: Click any commit in your repository’s Commits tab on GitHub, and you can leave a comment directly on it, useful for asking “why did you change this line?” or leaving feedback.
Creating an Issue: On your repository’s GitHub page, click the Issues tab → New issue. Issues are used to track bugs, questions, or tasks, for example, “Script fails when df has missing values.” Give it a clear title and description.
Resolving an Issue: Once the problem is fixed (perhaps in a later commit), you can reference the issue number in your commit message (e.g., Fixes #3), which will automatically close it on GitHub once pushed. Alternatively, open the issue directly and click Close issue once resolved, optionally leaving a comment explaining the fix.


You now have the final piece of a reproducible, shareable workflow: your data, your code, your environment (via renv), and now your version history (via Git and GitHub), all able to travel together as a single, inspectable package.

Exercise 3.2:

Pair with a friend in class. Pull each other’s repository.
Your friend should open your project, run renv::restore(), and then try running your R script.
Is it reproducible? Did they get the exact same outputs? Discuss any differences and improve your script and renv setup as per your peer’s feedback.

title: From Workflow to Reproducible Report
section: A Quick Primer on Markdown Syntax
text:
A Quick Primer on Markdown Syntax
Before we look at .qmd files, you need to know Markdown, a simple way to format plain text using symbols instead of buttons (like you would in Word). You’ve likely never used it before, so here’s everything you need for this exercise:


What you type
What it becomes



# Heading 1
A large heading


## Heading 2
A smaller heading


**bold text**
bold text


*italic text*
italic text



- item or * item

A bullet point


1. item
A numbered list item


`code`
inline code font



That’s it. Markdown is just plain text with a few symbols sprinkled in. Quarto reads this and converts it into nicely formatted text in your final report.
crumbs: 16  From Workflow to Reproducible Report

title: From Workflow to Reproducible Report
text:
How Quarto Works
A Quarto document (a .qmd file) is a plain text file that blends narrative text (written in Markdown) with executable code chunks (e.g. R). When you “render” a .qmd file, Quarto executes the code, embeds the results (tables, plots, etc.) directly into your document, and converts it into your desired output format (like HTML, PDF, or Word).
A .qmd file has four key components:
1. YAML Header
Located at the very top of the file, enclosed by --- on both sides. It contains metadata like title, author, date, and format (e.g., html, pdf). This tells Quarto what kind of document to produce and how to label it.
2. Code Chunks
Blocks of executable R code, enclosed in triple backticks with curly braces specifying the language, like this:
```{r}
1 + 1
```
You can add options inside the curly braces to control how the chunk behaves, for example:


{r} — a standard, visible code chunk.

{r, echo=FALSE} — runs the code but hides the code itself in the report (only shows the output).

{r, eval=FALSE} — shows the code but does not run it.
3. Text
Narrative content written using the Markdown syntax above. This is where you explain your analysis, interpret results, and provide context (just like you would write in a lab report), but interwoven directly with your code and results.
4. Inline Code
Small snippets of R code embedded directly within a sentence of text, using a single backtick followed by r (see example below). This lets you report a single computed value (like a mean or p-value) directly in your sentence, so it updates automatically if your data changes.
crumbs: 16  From Workflow to Reproducible Report

title: From Workflow to Reproducible Report
text:
Example: A Minimal .qmd File
Below is a short, complete example containing all four components. Create a new file in RStudio (File → New File → Quarto Document, or just a plain text file saved with a .qmd extension) and paste this in:

---
title: "My First Quarto Report"
author: "Your Name"
date: "2026-10-10"
format: html
---

## Introduction

This report summarises a small example dataset to demonstrate how Quarto combines **code**, **text**, and *results* in one document.

## The Data

```{r}
df = data.frame(
  group = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  value = c(10, 15, 20, 25)
)

df
```

## Summary

```{r}
avg_value = mean(df$value)
avg_value
```

The average value across all groups is `r avg_value`. This sentence used **inline code** to insert that number automatically.

## Visualization

```{r}
plot(df$group, df$value, main = "Value by Group")
```

Rendering a .qmd File
Save your .qmd file and turn it into a finished report:

Ensure the .qmd file is open in RStudio (appear in the Source pane).
Look at the top of that pane. You’ll see a toolbar with a blue arrow icon and the word Render next to it (it’s a button, not a menu item). Click it.

Alternatively, use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl + Shift + K (Windows) or Cmd + Shift + K (Mac).


RStudio will run all the code chunks in order, then open a preview of your finished report (by default, in the Viewer pane, or in a separate window).
Check your project folder. You’ll find a new .html file with the same name as your .qmd file. This is the rendered report.

Tip: If rendering fails, RStudio will show you an error message in the Render tab at the bottom, usually pointing to the exact line and code chunk that caused the problem. Fix the code chunk, save, and click Render again.
Notice how the final rendered report will show your data table, the computed average written directly into a sentence, and a plot — all generated live from the code, not typed in by hand.

title: Real-world Public Health Analytical Workflows
text:
Building a Template Repo, Step-by-Step
Every project you start from here on will need the same basic scaffolding: an RStudio project, a Git repository, folders organized sensibly, and some baseline documentation. Rather than redoing this setup by hand every time, let’s build it once, carefully, as a template repository you can reuse for every future project.

title: Real-world Public Health Analytical Workflows
text:
Step 1: Create a New Repository on GitHub
Go to github.com, click the + icon (top right) → New repository, and configure it as follows:

Repository name: project-template
Public vs. Private: Choose Public for this exercise. A public repo is visible to anyone on the internet; a private repo is visible only to you and people you explicitly invite. For real research projects involving unpublished data or sensitive health information, you would almost always choose Private until you’re ready to share results publicly.
Start from a template: Choose No. This option would let you pre-fill the repo from an existing template repository, but since we’re building our own template from scratch today, we don’t need one yet.
Add a README file: Choose Yes. This creates a basic README.md immediately, so your repository isn’t empty, and gives you something to practice editing shortly.
Add .gitignore: Choose the R template from the dropdown. GitHub maintains a library of sensible .gitignore starting points per language; the R template pre-fills common R-specific clutter to ignore (like .Rhistory and .RData files), saving you from typing it out yourself.
Choose a license: This determines what others are legally allowed to do with your code. A few common options:

MIT License: Very permissive. Anyone can use, modify, or distribute your code, including commercially, as long as they credit you.
GNU GPLv3: Permissive but “viral”: anyone can use and modify your code, but anything they build using it must also be released under GPL and stay open-source.
No license: Legally, this means no one else has any rights to use, copy, or modify your code at all, even though it’s publicly visible on GitHub. This is often the default by accident, and rarely what people intend.

For this exercise, pick MIT, a reasonable default for teaching materials and most academic code.

Click Create repository.






Why does the license matter even for a class exercise?



You might not think much about licensing for a practice repo, but the habit matters. Public health code often gets reused by other researchers or public health units; an unclear or missing license can actually prevent otherwise-willing collaborators from legally reusing your work, even if that was never your intention.




Step 2: Clone the Repository to Your Computer
Back in RStudio, go to File → New Project → Version Control → Git, and paste in your repository’s URL (click the green Code button on your repo’s GitHub page to copy it). Choose a location to save it locally, and click Create Project.


Step 3: Explore What GitHub Already Gave You
Look at the Files pane in RStudio. Because of the options you chose during creation, your cloned repo already contains:

README.md: a short Markdown file, currently just the repo name. This is the first thing anyone sees when visiting your repository on GitHub.
.gitignore: a plain text file listing patterns of files Git should never track. Since you chose the R template, open it now and skim through; you’ll recognize some entries like .Rhistory and .Rproj.user/.
LICENSE: the full legal text of the MIT license you selected.

Notice that there is no .Rproj file yet. GitHub has no concept of RStudio Projects, it only knows about files and folders, so this step is still ours to do.


Step 4: Turn the Repo into an RStudio Project
Recall from Week 3: a Project fixes your working directory and keeps everything self-contained. Since you cloned via File → New Project → Version Control → Git, RStudio actually already created the .Rproj file for you automatically as part of that process, look in your Files pane for project-template.Rproj. If, for any reason, it isn’t there (for example, if you cloned using the Terminal or GitHub Desktop instead), you can create it manually: go to File → New Project → Existing Directory, and point RStudio to your cloned folder.


Step 5: Build Out the Folder Structure
A single analysis.R worked fine for small weekly exercises, but real projects accumulate many scripts for different purposes, and need a predictable place for each. Inside your project, create the following folders and empty placeholder files:
project-template/
├── project-template.Rproj
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── LICENSE
└── scripts/
    ├── data/
    │   ├── import/
    │   ├── process/
    │   └── explore/
    └── analysis/
You can create folders either through the Files pane (New Folder button) or directly in the Terminal tab:
mkdir -p scripts/data/import scripts/data/process scripts/data/explore scripts/analysis
Git does not track empty folders, only files, so each new folder will not actually appear in Git’s history until it contains something. A common convention is to drop a placeholder file (often named .gitkeep, an otherwise meaningless empty file whose only purpose is to make an empty folder trackable) inside each one for now:
touch scripts/data/import/.gitkeep scripts/data/process/.gitkeep scripts/data/explore/.gitkeep scripts/analysis/.gitkeep
Stage, commit, and push these changes through the Git pane as you’ve practiced before.


Step 6: Convert This Repository into a GitHub Template
Now that your structure is in place, let’s make it officially reusable. On your repository’s GitHub page, go to Settings, and under the General tab, tick the checkbox labeled Template repository.
From now on, anyone visiting your repo (including future-you) will see a green Use this template button instead of just Code. Clicking it creates a brand-new repository with this entire folder structure, README, .gitignore, and license already in place, but with a clean Git history, no inherited commits from today’s setup work. This is exactly the “start from a template: yes” option you declined back in Step 1, except now you’re the one providing the template for next time.

title: Real-world Public Health Analytical Workflows
section: .gitignore: What to NOT Track in Git
text:
.gitignore: What to NOT Track in Git
So far we’ve treated .gitignore as something GitHub generates for us. Now let’s understand what it actually does, and why some files belong there deliberately.

Why Deliberately Exclude Files?
Two categories of files are usually poor fits for Git tracking, even though it might feel natural to include everything:

Data files. Raw data is often large (Git is not designed to efficiently store large binary files, every version lives in history forever, bloating the repository), and in public health contexts, is frequently sensitive: patient records, identifiable survey responses, or data under a restrictive sharing agreement. Committing such data to a public GitHub repository, even by accident, can constitute a serious data breach.
Computed outputs. Rendered plots, generated tables, and intermediate processed datasets are usually products of your code applied to your data. Since they can always be reproduced by re-running your scripts, there is little reason to track every version of them in Git, and doing so adds clutter without adding information. Importantly, outputs can also indirectly leak sensitive information from the underlying data (for example, a summary table with very small cell counts in a demographic breakdown), so the same caution around sensitivity applies.

The general principle: track what can’t be regenerated (your code), and exclude what can (data and outputs).


Understanding .gitignore Syntax
A .gitignore file is just a plain text file, one pattern per line, placed at the root of your repository. A few core rules:

A plain filename (notes.txt) ignores any file with that exact name, anywhere in the repo.
A trailing slash (data/) ignores an entire folder and everything inside it.
A wildcard asterisk (*.csv) ignores every file matching that pattern, regardless of name.
A leading ! negates a pattern, meaning “don’t ignore this,” useful for carving out an exception within an otherwise-ignored folder.
Lines starting with # are comments and are ignored by Git itself.


Exercise 4.1:

Inside your project-template repo, create a new folder scripts/data/import/raw/ and place a dummy file inside it, for example touch scripts/data/import/raw/patient_data.csv.
Run git status in the Terminal tab. Confirm that Git currently sees this new file as untracked.
Open .gitignore and add a line to ignore this file specifically: scripts/data/import/raw/patient_data.csv. Run git status again; the file should no longer appear.
Now replace that line with a broader pattern, *.csv, so that any CSV file anywhere in the project is ignored. Create one or two more dummy .csv files in different folders, and confirm via git status that none of them show up as untracked.
Finally, add an exception: suppose you do want to track a small lookup table, scripts/data/import/raw/lookup_table.csv. Add a line !scripts/data/import/raw/lookup_table.csv beneath your *.csv line, and confirm via git status that this one file reappears as trackable while the others remain ignored.

title: An Example Template
text:
Forking the Template to Your Own GitHub
Before cloning sph5009-project-template to your computer, let’s get it onto your GitHub account first. Your instructor’s copy lives in their GitHub repository; to work with it, track your own changes, and push your own commits, you need your own copy of that repository on GitHub, linked back to the original.
This is exactly what forking does. A fork creates a full copy of someone else’s repository under your own account, complete with its entire commit history, but as an independent repository you fully own and control. You can commit, push, and modify your fork freely without affecting the original, and GitHub keeps track of the relationship between the two, so you can later open a Pull Request if you ever want to propose your changes back to the original repository (not required for this exercise, but it’s how most open-source collaboration works in practice).
Forking differs from the use_github() cloning you’ve done before in one key way: cloning on its own just downloads a copy of a repo to your computer, your local copy still points back at the original remote (origin), and you likely won’t have permission to push to it. Forking instead creates a new, separate repository on GitHub itself, one that you own and can push to, before you ever clone anything to your machine.

title: An Example Template
section: Symlinks: Having Data There but Not There
text:
Symlinks: Having Data There but Not There
Look closely at sph5009-project-template: there is no data/ folder. This is deliberate, not an oversight, and the root README.md’s “Data Sensitivity” section explains the reasoning in full. The short version:
Data files are excluded from Git entirely (recall Section 2), but a project that reads data still needs some consistent file path to read it from. The template’s solution is to keep the actual data in an external location outside the Git repo altogether (a shared drive, a secure data server, or similar), and create a symbolic link (“symlink”) inside the project that points to it. To your R scripts, the symlinked folder looks and behaves exactly like a normal local folder, read.csv("data/raw/survey.csv") works fine, but nothing about the data itself is ever tracked by Git, since Git only sees a tiny pointer file, not the data.
The exact command differs by operating system, but the README documents all three:

macOS / Linux: ln -s /path/to/external/data data
Windows (Command Prompt, as Administrator): mklink /D data C:\path\to\external\data
Windows (PowerShell): New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path data -Target C:\path\to\external\data

This solves access, but not provenance: if the data itself isn’t in Git, how do you prove which exact version of the data your results came from? The template’s answer is a hash manifest: data_manifest.csv at the project root records a cryptographic hash (a fixed-length fingerprint that changes if even one byte of the file changes) for each data file your project depends on. The script scripts/data/import/verify_data_hash.R recomputes the hash of your current data and compares it against the recorded value, flagging a mismatch if the data has changed since the hash was recorded.






Why a hash instead of just a filename or date?



Filenames and modification dates can be wrong or misleading. Someone could fix a typo in a dataset without renaming it, or your computer’s reported file date could be unreliable after copying between systems. A hash is a precise, bit-for-bit fingerprint, it cannot lie about whether the content has changed, even by one cell.



Exercise 4.3:

Create a small dummy dataset somewhere outside your sph5009-project-template folder (for example, ~/external-data/dummy.csv with a few made-up rows).
Create a symlink inside your project pointing data/ to that external folder, using the command appropriate to your operating system from the README.
Run scripts/data/import/generate_data_hash.R to compute a real hash for your dummy file and automatically write it into data_manifest.csv, replacing the placeholder value.
Edit your dummy CSV slightly (change one value), then run the verification script. Confirm it correctly flags a mismatch.
Run git status and confirm that your actual data file does not appear as trackable, only your updated data_manifest.csv and any script changes do. Only once you’ve verified this, stage and commit those changes.








Two scripts, two purposes



generate_data_hash.R computes hashes for your current data and writes them into data_manifest.csv, run this once when you first add data, or deliberately whenever the data legitimately changes. verify_data_hash.R does the opposite: it checks your current data against the manifest and reports a mismatch if something’s different. You (or a collaborator) will run verify_data_hash.R far more often than generate_data_hash.R, since generating a new hash should be a deliberate, rare action, not something run reflexively.

title: An Example Template
section: A Project Is More Than One Script
text:
A Project Is More Than One Script
As your pipeline grows (import, then process, then explore, then analyze), resist the temptation to cram everything into one ever-growing script. The sph5009-project-template demonstrates the main.R as table-of-contents pattern discussed earlier today: open main.R now and look at its contents.
Each stage of the pipeline lives in its own file, under the folder matching its purpose, and main.R simply source()s them in order. This has a few concrete advantages worth noticing as you read through it: you can re-run a single stage in isolation while developing (just run that one script directly, rather than the whole pipeline); each file is small enough to understand at a glance.

Exercise 4.4:

In sph5009-project-template, add a new script under scripts/data/process/ that performs one additional transformation of your choosing on the data from Exercise 4.3 (for example, filtering out rows, or adding a derived column).
Add a source() line for your new script into main.R, in the correct position in the pipeline.
Re-run main.R end to end and confirm it still runs without errors, and that your new processing step took effect.
Commit and push your changes, with a commit message describing what you added.

title: Real-world Reports
text:
Rendering from main.R
Quarto documents can be rendered programmatically, from R itself, using the quarto package:
Add a line like this to the end of your main.R, after your analysis steps, and your final report becomes just another stage of the pipeline, generated automatically every time main.R runs end-to-end.

title: Real-world Reports
section: 7. Tweaking Rendered Output: From Script to Report
text:
7. Tweaking Rendered Output: From Script to Report
A rendered .qmd using entirely default settings tends to look like a script with some text around it: every chunk’s code is visible, every warning and message prints inline, and plots appear at whatever size Quarto happens to pick. A real report, the kind you’d hand to a stakeholder who doesn’t code, needs these tweaked deliberately.

Chunk Options: echo, eval, warning, and Friends
Each code chunk accepts options, written as #| comment lines at the top of the chunk, that control what appears in the rendered output:
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

summary_table =
  df %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(mean_value = mean(value))

echo: false hides the code itself, showing only its output. Use this for any chunk your final audience doesn’t need to see to understand the result.
eval: false shows the code but does not run it, useful for documentation or demonstrating syntax without executing it.
warning: false and message: false suppress R’s warning and message output from cluttering the report. Errors are not suppressed by default, you generally want to know if something actually broke.

You can also set these options once, for the entire document, in the YAML header, and override them for individual chunks as needed:
---
title: "Monthly Surveillance Report"
format: html
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---


Controlling Plot Size
Default plot dimensions rarely look right in a finished report; figures often render too small to read, or too large relative to surrounding text. Set figure dimensions (in inches) per chunk:
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of values by group"

ggplot(df, aes(x = group, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot()
fig-cap adds a proper, numbered caption beneath the figure, a small touch that makes a substantial difference in how polished the final document feels.


Using QMD Templates for Consistent Formatting
If you (or your team) produce the same style of report repeatedly, it’s worth creating a template .qmd with your preferred YAML defaults (theme, table of contents settings, standard chunk options) already filled in, so you’re not re-configuring formatting from scratch every time. A minimal example:
---
title: "Report Title"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: cosmo
    code-fold: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---
code-fold: true is a nice middle ground for technical audiences: it hides code by default but keeps it one click away via a small toggle, rather than removing it from the document entirely.
cosmo is just one of many built-in themes Quarto ships with via the Bootswatch library; others worth trying include flatly (clean, muted colors, popular for reports), litera (serif-leaning, reads like a printed document), journal (bold headers, magazine-like), and darkly (dark mode). Swapping between them is just a matter of changing the one word after theme: in your YAML header, so it’s worth trying a few against your own report to see what reads best, rather than defaulting to the first one you saw.

Exercise 4.6:

In report.qmd in Exercise 4.5, set echo: false and warning: false at the document level, in the YAML header.
In any plot-producing chunk in your report, explicitly set fig-width, fig-height, and fig-cap.
Re-render the report (via main.R, as in Exercise 4.5) and compare it to the earlier version. In 2-3 sentences, note what changed and whether it reads more like a polished report now.




Rendering to PDF and Word
Everything above works identically regardless of output format, echo, fig-width, params, and the rest all carry over unchanged. The only thing that changes is the format field in your YAML header. So far you’ve been rendering to html, but for public health reporting, your actual audience (a supervisor, a health department, a policy team) will often expect a Word document they can mark up with track changes, or a PDF they can archive, print, or email as a fixed, non-editable record.
Switching is a one-line change:
---
title: "Monthly Surveillance Report"
format: docx
---
---
title: "Monthly Surveillance Report"
format: pdf
---
You can even render to multiple formats from the exact same .qmd, with no duplicated code, by listing them together:
---
title: "Monthly Surveillance Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
  docx: default
  pdf: default
---
Running quarto::quarto_render("report.qmd") with this header produces an .html, .docx, and .pdf version in one call, all from the same source file and the same underlying data.






PDF rendering needs LaTeX



Unlike HTML and Word, PDF output requires a LaTeX installation on your machine, which most people don’t have by default. The first time you try to render to PDF, you may see an error about a missing LaTeX engine. Quarto provides a lightweight, R-friendly way to install one:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
You only need to do this once per machine.








Matching a house style in Word



By default, .docx output uses Quarto’s generic styling. If your institution has a standard Word template (specific fonts, header/footer, logo), you can point Quarto at it instead of starting from a blank style:
format:
  docx:
    reference-doc: my-institution-template.docx
Quarto will copy the styles (headings, body text, tables) from my-institution-template.docx into your rendered output, so your report matches house style without manual reformatting after the fact.



Exercise 4.7:

In report.qmd from Exercise 4.6, change the format field to render to docx instead of html.
Re-render via main.R and open the resulting Word document. Confirm your chunk options (echo: false, figure captions, etc.) carried over correctly.
If you have a LaTeX distribution installed (or are willing to install tinytex), try rendering to pdf as well, using the multi-format YAML syntax shown above, so that main.R produces .html, .docx, and .pdf versions from a single render call.


Alternatively, you don’t need to edit the file at all to render a different format one time. quarto_render() accepts an output_format argument that overrides the YAML for that call only:
quarto::quarto_render("report.qmd", output_format = "docx")
This is a handy way to keep a single default format in your .qmd for everyday use (quick previews while writing, say), while still being able to generate a Word or PDF version on demand from main.R without touching the source file, an example of the same principle from Exercise 4.5’s execute_params argument: keep the .qmd itself stable, and control variation from the calling R code instead.

Congrats! You’ve now built a complete, real-world analytical workflow: a structured repo created from a reusable template, data handled safely outside of Git with provenance tracked via hashes, a modular pipeline orchestrated from a single main.R, and a parameterized, polished report generated as its final output.

title: Best Practices in Using Coding Support Tools
text:
AI Assistance
AI assistance in coding is not a single, uniform thing. It shows up in several distinct forms, each with its own risks and appropriate uses.
crumbs: 20  Best Practices in Using Coding Support Tools

title: Best Practices in Using Coding Support Tools
text:
Chat: Copy-Paste
The most familiar form is simply chatting with an AI model in a separate window, then copying its output into your script. You are probably already doing this, pasting an error message into a chat window and copying back a fix, or asking for a function and transplanting it into your .R or .qmd file. It is simple and flexible, but because the AI’s output is detached from your actual working file, it is easy to lose track of why a particular piece of code was suggested, and whether it still fits once you have made further edits.


Auto-Complete
Auto-complete used to be a modest convenience: your editor would suggest a function name, close a bracket, or complete a variable you had already typed elsewhere. It was predictable and easy to verify at a glance.
Modern auto-complete is a different beast entirely. It can now generate whole chunks of code, a full dplyr pipeline, an entire ggplot2 call, even a small function, based on a few words of context or a comment you wrote. This raises an important question you should always ask yourself: are these AI guesses really what you intended? The suggestion may run without error and even produce plausible-looking output, while still subtly misrepresenting your data, using the wrong grouping variable, or silently dropping missing values in a way you did not intend. The fluency of the output does not guarantee its correctness.


Agentic Coding
The most powerful, and most hands-off, form of AI assistance is agentic coding, where the AI is given a broader goal and allowed to plan, write, and sometimes execute multiple steps on its own. This generally takes one of two shapes:

Incremental: the agent works in small, reviewable steps, pausing for your input or confirmation along the way.
One-shot: the agent is given a task and produces a complete solution in a single pass, with no intermediate checkpoints.

The more autonomy you hand over, the more deliberate you need to be about how you direct and review that work.

title: Local LLM and RStudio
text:
Step 1: Install Ollama (one-time, outside R)
Ollama is a free, open-source application that downloads, manages, and runs open LLMs (such as Llama, Qwen, or Mistral) directly on your own computer. Once a model is downloaded, it runs fully offline, with no internet connection or API key required.

title: Local LLM and RStudio
text:
Go to https://ollama.com/download and install Ollama for your operating system.
Confirm it installed correctly by opening a terminal and running:

ollama --version

title: Local LLM and RStudio
section: Step 2: Pull a local model (one-time, outside R)
text:
Step 2: Pull a local model (one-time, outside R)
https://ollama.com/search lists all the models you can interact with via ollama. In your terminal (not the R console), download a small code-capable model qwen2.5-coder:7b:
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

# Alternative models to try if your laptop has limited RAM:
# ollama pull llama3.2:3b
# ollama pull codellama:7b

Tip: qwen2.5-coder:7b needs ~5-6 GB RAM. If your laptop struggles, use llama3.2:3b instead.

title: Local LLM and RStudio
text:
Step 3: Install the R packages

install.packages(c("ellmer", "chattr"))



ellmer is the underlying engine. It handles the actual connection to an LLM, local or cloud, sending your prompt to the model and returning the response as a usable R object.

chattr is the user-facing layer built on top of ellmer. It adds the RStudio-friendly interface: a chat app that opens in the Viewer pane, plus Addins like “Send prompt” that let you query the model without writing any connection code.

In short, ellmer does the talking to the model; chattr gives you a convenient way to talk to ellmer from inside RStudio.

title: Local LLM and RStudio
section: Step 4: Configure chattr to use your local Ollama model
text:
Step 4: Configure chattr to use your local Ollama model

library(chattr)

# set chattr's backend to the local Ollama model you pulled
chattr_use("ollama/qwen2.5-coder:7b")

# quick connectivity check: sends a prompt and prints the response in the console
chattr("Write an R function that calculates BMI given weight in kg and height in m.")

Under the hood, chattr_use() configures ellmer for you. If it does not recognise the "ollama/..." shorthand (this interface has shifted across package versions), configure ellmer directly instead:

# If chattr_use() doesn't recognise "ollama/...", configure ellmer directly:
library(ellmer)

chat <- chat_ollama(model = "qwen2.5-coder:7b")
chattr_use(chat)

# try connectivity check again: sends a prompt and prints the response in the console
chattr("Write an R function that calculates BMI given weight in kg and height in m.")

title: Local LLM and RStudio
section: Step 5: Your first interaction, via the Shiny gadget
text:
Step 5: Your first interaction, via the Shiny gadget

Run chattr_app() in R console. A chat panel opens in the RStudio Viewer pane.
Type the following prompt into the chat box:


“Write an R function that calculates BMI given weight in kg and height in m.”


Review the code the model returns, then copy it into a script to test it.

title: Local LLM and RStudio
section: Step 6: Your first interaction, via the RStudio Add-in
text:
Step 6: Your first interaction, via the RStudio Add-in

In a new .R script, type a plain-English question as a comment:


# Write an R function `bmi_category` that flags BMI values as underweight, normal,
# overweight, or obese based on standard WHO cutoffs


Highlight that comment line.
Go to Addins → chattr: Send prompt (or use the keyboard shortcut if configured).
The response appears in the chattr panel; copy the generated function back into your script.

title: Local LLM and RStudio
text:
Step 7: See what’s actually sent
So far, chattr has sent your prompt plus some additional context (like surrounding script content) without showing you what that looks like. Use preview = TRUE to see the full payload without calling the model:

# Normal use: sends the prompt (plus context) to the model and returns a response
chattr("Write an R function that calculates BMI given weight in kg and height in m.")

# Dry run: shows the exact text/context that would be sent, without calling the model
chattr(
  "Write an R function that calculates BMI given weight in kg and height in m."
  , preview = TRUE
)

Compare the two outputs. What extra context, if any, got added to your prompt?

title: Local LLM and RStudio
text:
Step 8: Test the generated code

# Paste the AI-generated function here and test it
bmi_category(weight = 70, height = 1.75)

text:
Step 9: Reflect
In 2-3 sentences, note:

Did the local model’s code run correctly on the first try?
How did the response compare to what you’d expect from a cloud model like ChatGPT or Claude?
What are the privacy/speed trade-offs you noticed?

title: What is Scaffolding?
text:
Step-by-Step Guide to Scaffolding
1. Discuss project structure with AI
Before any code is written, talk through the shape of the project with the AI, treating it as a sounding board rather than a builder.
2. Set up the folder structure
Translate the discussion above into an actual, if mostly empty, folder and file layout. This is still just words and placeholders, no real logic yet.
3. Add comments
Inside each empty or near-empty file, write comments describing what that file is supposed to do, before any function body exists.
4. Define function names and interfaces (inputs, outputs)
Decide, and write down, the names of your key functions and what goes in and comes out of each one. You are not implementing the logic yet, only pinning down the contract each function must honor.

title: What is Scaffolding?
text:
Ask for critiques of existing projects or structures, especially if you are working in a domain that is unfamiliar to you. Show the AI a folder layout or an existing script and ask it to point out weaknesses, rather than asking it to design from scratch.
Do not let the AI implement anything at this stage. It will keep pushing to write code for you, because that is what it is optimized to do. Resist that. Your job here is to think, not to produce.

title: What is Scaffolding?
section: Example: A Scaffold for a Simple Analysis Project

Example: A Scaffold for a Simple Analysis Project
Let’s extend last week’s to have scaffold inside it, deciding what each script is responsible for and what it hands off to the next.
project-template/

├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── LICENSE
└── scripts/
    ├── data/
    │   ├── import/

title: What is Scaffolding?
text:
Micro One-Shot
Carlos’s own practice, once the architecture is settled, is to hand a large task to the agent in a single pass and let it produce a complete solution in one shot. For many of us, though, reviewing a one-shot of an entire project in one sitting can be daunting. The diff is enormous, your attention inevitably drifts, and subtle problems slip through simply because there is too much to hold in your head at once. Also, for a local AI model, large one-shot generations tend to perform poorly compared to their cloud counterparts, since local models are typically smaller and less capable of holding an entire project’s context in mind at once.
So here, we adapt Carlos’s philosophy to micro one-shots, keeping the underlying principle, clear boundaries before execution, while shrinking the scale at which we apply it:

Still write a good scaffold first. This part does not change.
One-shot small, digestible sections, one function, one file, one well-defined chunk at a time, rather than the whole project at once.
Review the output, run it, and if it does not work or you cannot fully understand it, throw it away and revise your instructions rather than patching broken code you do not understand.

This keeps the review burden manageable, works even on local models with limited context, and still gives you the core benefit of scaffolding: you always know what each piece is supposed to do before the AI writes it.

1. Create a new R project
Set up a new R project as we covered in earlier sessions.

title: Final Exercise
section: 2. Create main.R at the root of your project directory
text:
2. Create main.R at the root of your project directory
main.R acts as a single entry point for your whole pipeline: it documents, in order, every step your project involves, and runs each one by sourcing the corresponding script. Populate it with comments describing your planned steps, then write out the source() calls needed to execute each script in order, keeping in mind the directory and file structures you learnt last week. For example:
# clean data: import raw data from data/raw, clean it, and write for downstream use
source('scripts/data/cases/process.R')  # output to: data/processed

# data exploration plots
source('scripts/explore/cases.R')       # output to: output/explore

# analyse data
source('scripts/analyse/stats.R')       # output to: output/stats
source('scripts/analyse/regression.R')  # output to: output/regression

# synthesize report from all exploration and analyses
source('scripts/report/prelim.R')

section: 3. Create directories and empty files as per your main.R
text:
3. Create directories and empty files as per your main.R
Set up the folder structure and empty script files that your main.R refers to, so everything is in place before you start filling them in.

title: Final Exercise
section: 4. Build out each script, in procedural order
text:
4. Build out each script, in procedural order
Work through your files in the order your pipeline actually runs, starting with data cleaning and moving downstream from there.
4.1 Scaffold each file. For each file, populate it with rough scaffolds (comments) outlining the steps needed inside it.
4.2 Validate the plan with your LLM. Brainstorm with your LLM whether these steps make sense. Try asking for better ways to do it, and push back on its suggestions to see how it responds.
4.3 Define interfaces within one file. Once you are happy with the overall plan, go through the scaffolds in the script, one scaffold at a time, and ask the LLM to define the boundaries and interfaces of each step, that is, what inputs it needs and what outputs it should produce, whether that step ends up as a function, a block of code, or something else. Remember that you can mix R code with free text in scaffolding. The LLM should be able to handle this. Review and refine the scaffolds until the logic is clear and correct.
4.4 Micro one-shot each scaffold. Try micro one-shotting each scaffold: asking the LLM to generate the full implementation for just one small, well-defined function at a time, rather than the whole script at once. Converse with it along the way to learn from its reasoning, not just copy its output. Remember your good old ?help is also there to help you.

text:
Reflect
In 2 to 3 sentences, note:

Where did the local LLM help you most today, and where did it struggle?
Were there moments you wished you had a more capable cloud model instead? What made you feel that way?
How might you use this scaffold-and-verify workflow on your own projects going forward?
